duplicate-9dc0647d95c2bdde.hint: Try listing the known motion quantities first. Which constant-acceleration equation leaves only the quantity you need?
notes: For constant acceleration, use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² or v² = u² + 2as. Choose the equation that avoids an unknown you do not need.
Choose one positive direction and keep the signs of displacement, velocity and acceleration consistent. Speed is the magnitude of velocity.
“From rest” sets the initial velocity to zero. It does not say that the acceleration is zero.

duplicate-0738b0d27149fa97.hint: Compare the upward resistive force with the weight at each stage, rather than assuming the acceleration stays constant.
notes: Use resultant force = ma with a declared positive direction. Drag increases with speed in the stated model, while weight is essentially constant.
Terminal speed means balanced forces and zero acceleration; it does not mean zero speed. Opening a parachute can reverse the direction of acceleration before the motion reverses.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q4:whole.hint: Resolve forces parallel and perpendicular to the contact surface. Decide which way the object would tend to move.
notes: For a simple incline, weight has components mg sin θ down the plane and mg cos θ into it. Other applied forces can change the normal reaction.
Kinetic friction has magnitude μ_k N. Static friction adjusts up to μ_s N; use the maximum only at impending slip, and choose its direction to oppose relative slipping.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q5:whole.hint: The spring force changes as the spring stretches. How is that represented on a force–extension graph?
notes: For a Hooke’s-law spring, F = kx and elastic energy = ½kx². Here x is extension or compression from the natural length.
When spring, kinetic and gravitational energy all change, include all three stores. Do not use F_final x for the spring’s work.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q6:whole.hint: Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after, using the supplied velocities or momentum result.
notes: Add ½mv² for every moving object in each state. Energy dissipated is initial kinetic energy minus final kinetic energy.
Use E_k = p²/(2m) when momentum is supplied. Do not assume equal momenta imply equal kinetic energies for different masses.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q7:whole.hint: Decide whether the question asks for energy over an interval or the rate of transfer at one instant.
notes: Average power is energy transferred / time. Instantaneous mechanical power is P = Fv cos θ.
With a constant driving force, power still changes when speed changes. With constant power, driving force decreases as speed increases.

duplicate-d689a7570b613016.hint: Connect the energy supplied during the chosen interval to the temperature rise over that same interval.
notes: With negligible losses, Pt = mcΔT, so a temperature–time slope is P/(mc). Use a representative straight-line section of the graph.
If heat loss is included, use net heating power. A plateau during a phase change uses latent heat, not mcΔT with a zero temperature rise.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q9:whole.hint: Ask which observation each model can explain, rather than assuming one model explains every experiment.
notes: Interference and diffraction show wave behaviour; the photoelectric effect shows quantized energy transfer. Use the model suited to the observation.
Wave–particle duality does not mean every classical wave property and every classical particle property are observed simultaneously in one measurement.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q10:whole.hint: Identify what stays fixed: amount of gas, temperature, pressure or volume. Use only the simplification that those conditions allow.
notes: Use pV = nRT = NkT with absolute pressure and kelvin temperature. For a fixed amount, p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.
If gas leaks or moves between containers, the amount in one container may change. Apply conservation of total molecules to the complete closed system instead of assuming pV/T is fixed locally.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q11:whole.hint: Compare the acceleration with displacement from equilibrium, including its direction.
notes: Simple harmonic motion satisfies a = −ω²x: acceleration is proportional to displacement and points towards equilibrium. ω = 2πf = 2π/T.
Displacement is measured from equilibrium, not necessarily from the spring’s natural length. At equilibrium acceleration is zero while speed is greatest.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q12:whole.hint: Identify whether the diagram shows a snapshot across space or the motion of one point over time.
notes: Use v = fλ and f = 1/T. A spatial separation between equal-phase points gives wavelength; a time separation gives period.
Wave speed is the speed of a disturbance, not the speed of one oscillating particle. Keep the wave’s travel direction separate from the direction of particle motion.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q14:whole.hint: Mark the boundary conditions at both ends, then fit the simplest allowed pattern between them.
notes: Fixed string ends and closed pipe ends are displacement nodes; an open pipe end is a displacement antinode. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and adjacent antinode are λ/4 apart.
Two like ends allow L = nλ/2. One open and one closed end allows L = (2n − 1)λ/4. Use the mode shown, not automatically the fundamental.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q15:whole.hint: Connect current to the amount of charge transferred during the relevant time.
notes: Current is I = ΔQ/Δt. For repeated pulses use charge per pulse times pulses per second to obtain average current.
Convert ampere-hours to coulombs using 1 Ah = 3600 C. For microscopic motion use I = nqAv_d, distinguishing number density from total number of carriers.

duplicate-b639a5e097956e3b.hint: Distinguish the energy supplied per coulomb by the source from the voltage available across its terminals.
notes: For a discharging cell, ε = I(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε − Ir. Internal resistance dissipates some of the source’s power.
A graph of terminal V against I has intercept ε and gradient −r. Check whether the cell is delivering or receiving current before using the voltage sign.

notes: For a discharging cell, ε = I(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε − Ir. Internal resistance dissipates some of the source’s power.
A graph of terminal V against I has intercept ε and gradient −r. Check whether the cell is delivering or receiving current before using the voltage sign.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q18:whole.hint: Identify the geometry producing the field before choosing its formula or hand rule.
notes: For a long straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr); for a long ideal solenoid, B = μ₀nI. Here n is turns per unit length.
Use a right-hand grip rule with conventional current. Add fields as vectors, including cancellation between competing contributions.

duplicate-38b702f4f863e7c2.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

duplicate-bb0c0874695963b0.hint: Combine the allowed angular momentum with the orbit or energy relation given in the question.
notes: In the Bohr model, mvr = nℏ and Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force. These give r_n proportional to n² and energy proportional to −1/n².
For an orbital period, use 2πr/v. A photon from a transition uses the level-energy difference; its frequency is not generally the classical orbit frequency.

duplicate-67846e76352aefe7.hint: Compare the total mass or binding energy of the initial particles with that of the final particles.
notes: Energy released is (mass_initial − mass_final)c². Equivalently, it is the increase in total binding energy, not simply the difference in binding energy per nucleon.
When given binding energy per nucleon, multiply by the nucleon number first. Keep atomic and nuclear masses consistent so electron masses cancel correctly.

duplicate-d5d323f3ea970fbe.hint: Identify the useful output and the total input before forming a ratio.
notes: Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, or the corresponding power ratio. Both sides must refer to the same interval.
For several stages, multiply the stage efficiencies. Multiply by 100 only when giving a percentage.

duplicate-7b4589da961298a7.hint: Check the emitting area and use absolute temperature. The temperature dependence is much stronger than linear.
notes: Thermal emission power is P = εσAT⁴. For a sphere use 4πR²; for a black body ε = 1.
For ratios, keep any changes in emissivity and area as well as the fourth power of temperature. Net exchange with surroundings at Tₛ is εσA(T⁴ − Tₛ⁴) in the stated simple model.

duplicate-bd7d79dfba616c68.hint: Think about how energy passes between neighbouring particles, and whether mobile electrons are present.
notes: Conduction transfers energy without bulk movement of matter. In metals, mobile electrons and lattice interactions both contribute; a gas does not have a metallic lattice.
For a steady uniform slab, transfer rate is kAΔT/L. Larger area or temperature difference increases the rate; greater thickness decreases it.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q26:whole.hint: Check whether the question compares amplitude, intensity, or total power; these do not scale in the same way.
notes: For the same medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. For an isotropic point source, I = P/(4πr²).
When coherent waves overlap, add their signed displacements first and then square the resultant amplitude. Adding intensities alone loses the interference effect.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q27:whole.hint: Compare the two path lengths to the observation point. Does their difference reinforce or oppose the waves?
notes: For initially in-phase sources, constructive interference has path difference nλ; destructive interference has (n + ½)λ.
For a double slit at small angles, fringe spacing is λD/d. Use slit separation d, not slit width, and distinguish adjacent-fringe spacing from distance to a particular order.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q29:whole.hint: First decide whether the source and observer are getting closer or farther apart.
notes: For sound, source motion changes the spacing of wavefronts; observer motion changes how quickly they are encountered. Choose the Doppler signs so approach increases observed frequency.
For collinear motion, f_obs = f_source(v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source), with speeds measured relative to the medium. Do not simply exchange source and observer speeds.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q30:whole.hint: Ask whether the required quantity is energy, energy per coulomb, or force per coulomb.
notes: Electric potential is energy per unit charge: V = E_p/q. For a point charge V = kQ/r, and contributions add as signed scalars.
Electric field is perpendicular to equipotentials and points towards decreasing potential. Moving along an equipotential requires no change in electric potential energy.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q32:whole.hint: Compare the starting total mechanical energy with the minimum needed to reach infinity.
notes: With zero potential at infinity, the minimum escape condition is ½mv_e² − GMm/R = 0, so v_e = √(2GM/R).
Escape speed is different from circular orbital speed at the same radius. For ratios, use √(M/R); the escaping object’s mass cancels.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q33:whole.hint: Distinguish energy per kilogram from the energy of the whole object.
notes: With zero at infinity, gravitational potential is V_g = −GM/r and potential energy is mV_g. Work required for a slow move is m(V_final − V_initial).
Potential is a scalar, so add its contributions algebraically. Use mgΔh only for a small height change where g is approximately uniform.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q34:whole.hint: Decide whether the original flux is increasing or decreasing before choosing the induced field direction.
notes: Lenz’s law makes the induced effect oppose the change in flux. It need not oppose the original field when that field is decreasing.
Use the required induced field direction first, then the right-hand grip rule for conventional current. The opposition is consistent with energy conservation.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q35:whole.hint: Mark the potential difference across the component and the current through it. Are these the quantities given?
notes: For a resistor, V = IR. Series components carry the same current; parallel branches have the same potential difference.
Simplify a resistor network from the innermost series or parallel combination outwards. Resistances add in series; conductances 1/R add in parallel.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q37:whole.hint: Consider the energy carried by one photon and the energy needed to release one electron.
notes: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is hf = φ + E_k,max. At threshold, hf₀ = φ; a stopping potential gives E_k,max = eV_stop.

Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons; frequency changes the maximum kinetic energy. Below threshold, greater intensity cannot compensate for insufficient photon energy.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q38:whole.hint: Keep the proton count, neutron count and total nucleon count separate.
notes: Isotopes share proton number Z but differ in neutron number. Stability depends on the neutron-to-proton balance and competition between nuclear attraction and proton repulsion.
Nuclear radius scales approximately as A^(1/3), giving roughly constant nuclear density. Outer electrons control chemical behaviour; the nucleus controls radioactive properties.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q39:whole.hint: Connect the particle’s wavelength to its momentum, rather than treating it as a photon.
notes: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. For a non-relativistic particle, p = mv or √(2mE_k).

If accelerated from rest through a voltage magnitude V, E_k = |q|V. Use this only in the non-relativistic regime; E = hc/λ is a photon relation, not a general massive-particle kinetic-energy equation.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q40:whole.hint: Compare the elapsed time with the half-life, or express the remaining amount as a fraction of the initial amount.
notes: N = N₀e^(−λt), A = λN, and T_half = ln 2/λ. After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (½)^n.

sup-064316255265a882-0SL1q1:whole.hint: Carry out the calculation without rounding, then compare the precision of the measurements used.

sup-064316255265a882-0SL1q21:whole.hint: Find the angle between the conventional current and the magnetic field.
notes: A straight current-carrying segment experiences F = BIL sin θ. Use the length actually within the field.
Use the current direction for the force hand rule. The magnetic force is perpendicular to both current and field; a segment parallel to the field has no magnetic force.

A working turbine cannot remove all the air’s kinetic energy: air must keep moving away downstream. Include the stated efficiency rather than assuming complete extraction.

notes: On a displacement–time graph, gradient gives velocity. On a velocity–time graph, gradient gives acceleration and signed area gives displacement.

At the top and bottom of a vertical circle the weight contributes with different radial signs. At loss of contact or a just-taut string, set the contact force or tension to zero.

sup-59a633a1a2b93971-q9:whole.hint: Use the rotational counterparts of force, mass and acceleration. Is the torque constant?

sup-59a633a1a2b93971-q10:whole.hint: Start from the definition of γ and rearrange for v/c before substituting.

duplicate-b4d4593abf97ba97.hint: Compare the particle arrangement or energy-transfer rate, rather than assuming a sensation tells you the temperature.
notes: Temperature and rate of energy transfer are different. Metal can feel colder than plastic at the same temperature because it conducts energy away from skin faster.
Particle spacing and arrangement determine volume and density. Most solids are denser than their liquids, but water is a notable exception.

duplicate-e905e8edd3862581.hint: Write the ideal-gas equation in a form involving mass per unit volume.
notes: Using n = m/M and ρ = m/V gives p = ρRT/M. Keep molar mass M in kg mol⁻¹ when using SI units.

sup-1aff23cca0941015-q3:whole.hint: Start from the definition of γ and rearrange for v/c before substituting.

sup-1aff23cca0941015-q4:whole.hint: Which observer measures the object at rest? That observer measures its proper length.

sup-1aff23cca0941015-q5:whole.hint: Write down the position and time of each event in the frame where they are given before transforming them.

A phase change alters intermolecular potential energy; temperature tracks average random kinetic energy. Evaporation can cool the remaining liquid as energetic molecules escape.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q6:whole.hint: Connect the energy supplied during the chosen interval to the temperature rise over that same interval.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q7:whole.hint: Separate the power emitted by the star from the power received per unit area at the observer.
notes: For isotropic emission, apparent brightness b = L/(4πd²). With parallax p in arcseconds, distance in parsecs is d = 1/p.

sup-7f96227fe6ee20c6-q2:whole.hint: Separate the reflected part of the incoming sunlight from the part that is absorbed.

Use the same system boundary for numerator and denominator. For a planet, add reflected contributions that leave the planet; do not count outgoing infrared as reflected sunlight.

sup-7f96227fe6ee20c6-q3:whole.hint: Compare the wavelengths of incoming sunlight and radiation emitted by the cooler surface.

After an increase in infrared absorption, the planet warms until outgoing energy again matches absorbed sunlight. Avoid describing the greenhouse effect as reflection of all heat or destruction of energy.

sup-3d435c8ce48831da-q1:whole.hint: Draw the direction towards each attracting mass and measure distances from the centres of the masses.
notes: Outside a spherical mass, g = GM/r² and F = mg. Add field contributions as vectors when more than one mass is present.
An altitude above a surface is not the radius in the formula: r = R + h. The test mass affects force but not the field strength at its position.

sup-3d435c8ce48831da-q2:whole.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

sup-3d435c8ce48831da-q10:whole.hint: Look for a point where the two field contributions have opposite directions before equating their magnitudes.
notes: At a gravitational field null between two masses, GM₁/r₁² = GM₂/r₂², with r₁ + r₂ equal to their separation.
The point lies closer to the smaller mass. Zero field does not imply zero potential, because potential contributions add as signed scalars.

sup-471144013f4a171f-q1:whole.hint: Distinguish energy per kilogram from the energy of the whole object.
notes: With zero at infinity, gravitational potential is V_g = −GM/r and potential energy is mV_g. Work required for a slow move is m(V_final − V_initial).
Potential is a scalar, so add its contributions algebraically. Use mgΔh only for a small height change where g is approximately uniform.

sup-45e9b39ec46a9e4c-q1:whole.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

sup-45e9b39ec46a9e4c-q2:whole.hint: The conductor can redistribute its charges even if its net charge stays zero.
notes: A nearby charge polarizes a neutral conductor: opposite charge is attracted towards the nearer side and like charge moves farther away.
Because electric forces depend on distance, equal amounts of separated positive and negative charge need not produce cancelling forces on the nearby charge.

sup-45e9b39ec46a9e4c-q3:whole.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.

sup-45e9b39ec46a9e4c-q5:whole.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).
A magnetic field alone does no work: the force is perpendicular to velocity. Reverse the force direction for a negative charge.

sup-45e9b39ec46a9e4c-q6:whole.hint: Try placing a positive test charge at a few points to check the proposed field direction.
notes: Electric field lines point from positive towards negative charges, and their tangent gives the local field direction. Closer lines represent a stronger field.
Magnetic field lines form continuous loops. Field lines do not cross, because the field has one direction at each point.

sup-45e9b39ec46a9e4c-q7:whole.hint: Identify the geometry producing the field before choosing its formula or hand rule.
notes: For a long straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr); for a long ideal solenoid, B = μ₀nI. Here n is turns per unit length.
Use a right-hand grip rule with conventional current. Add fields as vectors, including cancellation between competing contributions.

Use the direction of entry or exit to determine the induced effect. A uniform field with no changing enclosed flux is not enough by itself to produce a circulating emf.

sup-9690687ab15d5eb9-q61:whole.hint: Translate “isothermal” into a statement about temperature, then consider what that means for an ideal gas’s internal energy.

sup-9690687ab15d5eb9-q62:whole.hint: Treat the gas as the system and mark the directions of heat and work before substituting numbers.
notes: With W positive for work done by the gas and Q positive into it, ΔU = Q − W. “Rejects heat” makes Q negative; compression makes W negative.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature. An unchanged temperature does not by itself mean no heat or work transfer.

sup-9690687ab15d5eb9-q64:whole.hint: Work is connected to the change in volume. On a pressure–volume graph, look for the relevant area.

notes: For a small-angle simple pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g). L runs from the suspension point to the bob’s centre of mass.

sup-c612dc14aaf01079-q2:whole.hint: Compare the acceleration with displacement from equilibrium, including its direction.
notes: Simple harmonic motion satisfies a = −ω²x: acceleration is proportional to displacement and points towards equilibrium. ω = 2πf = 2π/T.
Displacement is measured from equilibrium, not necessarily from the spring’s natural length. At equilibrium acceleration is zero while speed is greatest.

sup-c612dc14aaf01079-q3:whole.hint: Use the amplitude to fix the total energy, then compare the position with equilibrium.
notes: For SHM, v² = ω²(A² − x²), and total energy is ½mω²A². The kinetic energy depends on how far the oscillator is from equilibrium.
At a turning point speed is zero; at equilibrium its magnitude is ωA. Doubling amplitude changes total energy by a factor of four, not two.

sup-c612dc14aaf01079-q5:whole.hint: Find the effective stiffness that acts on the oscillating mass about its equilibrium position.
notes: For a mass on an ideal spring, T = 2π√(m/k). Adding springs or masses can change the effective k or m.
A constant gravitational force shifts the equilibrium of a vertical spring but does not change this ideal period. Keep extension from natural length separate from displacement about equilibrium.

sup-c612dc14aaf01079-q6:whole.hint: Use the initial displacement and initial direction of motion to decide where the oscillation starts.
notes: For x = A cos(ωt + φ), v = −ωA sin(ωt + φ) and a = −ω²x. Velocity is a quarter-cycle out of phase with displacement.

sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q3:whole.hint: Look for a point where the two field contributions have opposite directions before equating their magnitudes.

sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q6:whole.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q7:whole.hint: Choose the object or system and identify the resultant force, rather than using one force on its own.
notes: Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma. Resolve into independent directions; zero acceleration requires zero resultant force in that direction.
Newton’s third-law forces act on different bodies and are the same kind of interaction. Balanced forces act on the same body.

Account for any initial phase difference between the sources as well as the path difference. Equivalent phases differ by whole multiples of 2π.

duplicate-47b7223103a27057.hint: Find the effective stiffness that acts on the oscillating mass about its equilibrium position.
notes: For a mass on an ideal spring, T = 2π√(m/k). Adding springs or masses can change the effective k or m.
A constant gravitational force shifts the equilibrium of a vertical spring but does not change this ideal period. Keep extension from natural length separate from displacement about equilibrium.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q22:whole.hint: Compare the wavelength with the opening or obstacle size.
notes: Diffraction becomes more pronounced when the wavelength is comparable with the aperture size. For a single slit, minima satisfy a sin θ = nλ for nonzero integer n.
The central maximum extends to the first minimum on both sides. Its full angular width is approximately 2λ/a at small angles, not λ/a.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q23:whole.hint: Convert the quoted line density into the separation between adjacent grating lines.
notes: Grating maxima satisfy d sin θ = nλ. If there are N lines per metre, d = 1/N metres.
A possible order must have |sin θ| ≤ 1. Check whether the angle is from the central normal or between two maxima.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q24:whole.hint: The conductor can redistribute its charges even if its net charge stays zero.
notes: A nearby charge polarizes a neutral conductor: opposite charge is attracted towards the nearer side and like charge moves farther away.
Because electric forces depend on distance, equal amounts of separated positive and negative charge need not produce cancelling forces on the nearby charge.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q25:whole.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

duplicate-42c0885e524e3fab.hint: Identify the geometry producing the field before choosing its formula or hand rule.
notes: For a long straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2πr); for a long ideal solenoid, B = μ₀nI. Here n is turns per unit length.
Use a right-hand grip rule with conventional current. Add fields as vectors, including cancellation between competing contributions.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q27:whole.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

Use the required induced field direction first, then the right-hand grip rule for conventional current. The opposition is consistent with energy conservation.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q30:whole.hint: Distinguish energy per kilogram from the energy of the whole object.

duplicate-56fbad19b5ea7da4.hint: Identify the star’s initial mass and what fuel is being exhausted at the stage described.
notes: A star’s initial mass is the main determinant of its evolution. Low- and intermediate-mass stars can leave white dwarfs; sufficiently massive stars can undergo core-collapse supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes.
Distinguish the ejected material, such as a planetary nebula, from the surviving remnant. Main-sequence stars are sustained mainly by hydrogen fusion in their cores.

duplicate-08381c3b1a8899d4.hint: Find the difference between the two relevant energy levels, not the energy of just one level.
notes: For an atomic transition, photon energy is |E_final − E_initial| = hf = hc/λ. Downward transitions emit; upward transitions require absorption.
Use the positive magnitude of the gap, converting eV to J if using h in SI units. A larger gap corresponds to a shorter wavelength.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q35:whole.hint: Apply both energy and momentum conservation to the photon–electron interaction.
notes: For an initially stationary electron, the Compton wavelength shift is Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ), where θ is the photon scattering angle.
The outgoing photon energy is hc/λ′; the electron gains the difference from the incoming photon energy. The photon and electron scattering angles are not the same angle.

duplicate-8b8c5c1dc4c2ec21.hint: Match each reactor component to the quantity it changes: neutron speed, neutron number, or heat transfer.
notes: A moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb neutrons; coolant removes thermal energy. These are distinct functions.
A steady chain reaction requires, on average, one subsequent fission per fission event. Critical mass depends on neutron production, absorption and escape, including the material’s geometry.

duplicate-3b9cf287970d5d58.hint: Check which way surface temperature increases on the horizontal axis before locating the star.
notes: On a standard H–R diagram luminosity increases upwards and temperature increases to the left. Red giants are luminous but cool; white dwarfs are hot but faint.
Use L = 4πR²σT⁴ to compare radii. A hotter star is not necessarily more luminous, because emitting area also matters.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q38:whole.hint: Find the difference between the two relevant energy levels, not the energy of just one level.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q39:whole.hint: Consider the energy carried by one photon and the energy needed to release one electron.
notes: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is hf = φ + E_k,max. At threshold, hf₀ = φ; a stopping potential gives E_k,max = eV_stop.

Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons; frequency changes the maximum kinetic energy. Below threshold, greater intensity cannot compensate for insufficient photon energy.

sup-102f321caa4d59db-q40:whole.hint: Separate what the common small deflections tell you from what the rare large deflections tell you.
notes: Alpha scattering supports a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the atomic mass. Most particles pass through the largely empty atomic volume.
For a head-on closest-approach calculation, equate the initial kinetic energy to the increase in electric potential energy, using the alpha particle’s charge +2e.

sup-cb6437a8fa3a75c7-q23:whole.hint: Compare the elapsed time with the half-life, or express the remaining amount as a fraction of the initial amount.
notes: N = N₀e^(−λt), A = λN, and T_half = ln 2/λ. After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (½)^n.
Subtract background from measured count rates before finding a decay ratio. Activity counts decays per second; it is not the total number of undecayed nuclei.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q0:whole.hint: Both objects start from rest. Compare how falling distance depends on time before inserting the time ratio.
notes: For free fall from rest, h = ½gt². With the same g, the height ratio is the square of the time ratio.
Keep the requested order of the ratio: A to B is the inverse of B to A.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q1:whole.hint: After the initial push ends, which interaction could still exert a horizontal force on the trolley?
notes: An initial push changes momentum; it does not leave a continuing forward force. Once the hand is no longer touching, include only the remaining interactions.
Slowing forward motion requires a backward resultant force. Motion alone is not evidence of a forward force.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q2:whole.hint: Draw the three tensions acting on the ring and resolve the sloping tension horizontally and vertically.
notes: For the stationary ring, S cos θ = R and S sin θ = T, where θ is measured from the vertical.
Compare sin θ and cos θ for an angle below 45°, and remember that each component is smaller than the full vector.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q3:whole.hint: Choose a system containing the interacting objects and compare its total momentum before and after the event.
notes: When external impulse is negligible, Σmu = Σmv. Keep velocity signs, and apply the equation separately in each direction for a two-dimensional collision.
“Sticks together” gives one shared final velocity. Kinetic energy is conserved only for an elastic collision; momentum conservation alone does not make a collision elastic.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q4:whole.hint: Between bounces the acceleration is constant. At each impact the velocity reverses sign.
notes: A velocity–time graph for free flight has constant slope. A rebound produces a rapid jump across zero; it is not a smooth turning point.
Choose a positive direction consistently. With energy lost in successive bounces, the rebound speeds and flight intervals decrease.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q5:whole.hint: Compare wave speeds on the two sides and draw a normal at the boundary.
notes: A wave entering a slower medium bends towards the normal; entering a faster medium bends away. Frequency stays fixed, so wavelength changes in proportion to speed.
Wavefronts are perpendicular to rays. For parallel faces returning to the original medium, the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but can be displaced sideways.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q6:whole.hint: The outgoing and reflected microwaves form a stationary pattern. How far apart are neighbouring minima?
notes: The superposition of opposite-travelling waves produces nodes and antinodes. Adjacent intensity minima are separated by half a wavelength.
A node-to-neighbouring-antinode distance is one quarter wavelength; the question asks for minimum to minimum.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q7:whole.hint: Find the equivalent resistance of the two parallel lamps, then consider the voltage left across Z.
notes: Two identical lamps of resistance R in parallel have equivalent resistance R/2. Each lamp must have its rated voltage across it.
Z is in series with the parallel pair, so it carries their total current. Use the required voltage division rather than treating all three components as series resistors.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q8:whole.hint: The voltage is unchanged. Choose the power formula with voltage and resistance.
notes: At a fixed voltage, P = V²/R, so power is inversely proportional to resistance.
Do not use the fixed-current conclusion from P = I²R here: the current changes when the resistance changes.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q9:whole.hint: Focus on the original radioactive isotope, rather than all material remaining in the sample.
notes: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei of a specified isotope, or its activity, to fall to half its initial value.
Daughter products remain in the sample, so the total mass or volume need not halve.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q10:whole.hint: Separate what the common small deflections tell you from what the rare large deflections tell you.
notes: Alpha scattering supports a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the atomic mass. Most particles pass through the largely empty atomic volume.
For a head-on closest-approach calculation, equate the initial kinetic energy to the increase in electric potential energy, using the alpha particle’s charge +2e.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q11:whole.hint: Express the remaining activity as successive halvings.
notes: Activity follows the same fractional decay law as the number of undecayed parent nuclei. After n half-lives, A/A₀ = (½)^n.
Find the number of halvings first, then multiply by the stated half-life; do not multiply the half-life by the denominator of the fraction.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q12:whole.hint: Keep a separate account of nucleon number and electric charge on both sides of the decay.
notes: In alpha decay A decreases by 4 and Z by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton; in beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, with the appropriate emitted leptons.
Gamma emission changes nuclear energy without changing A or Z. Beta decay shares energy with a neutrino or antineutrino, giving a continuous beta spectrum.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q13:whole.hint: Keep the proton count, neutron count and total nucleon count separate.
notes: Isotopes share proton number Z but differ in neutron number. Stability depends on the neutron-to-proton balance and competition between nuclear attraction and proton repulsion.
Nuclear radius scales approximately as A^(1/3), giving roughly constant nuclear density. Outer electrons control chemical behaviour; the nucleus controls radioactive properties.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q16:whole.hint: The measured time is squared in the depth equation. How does this affect its fractional uncertainty?
notes: For d = ½gt² with g treated as exact, Δd/d = 2Δt/t.
Convert the fractional uncertainty back to an absolute depth uncertainty by multiplying by d. Do not round the intermediate fraction too early.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q17:whole.hint: Take logarithms of the proposed power law and compare it with the equation of a straight line.
notes: For F = kdⁿ, log F = log k + n log d. Plot the logarithms of both measured quantities; the gradient gives n and the intercept gives log k.
Recover k using the same logarithm base. Its units are N m^(−n), because kdⁿ must have force units.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q18:whole.hint: Separate the stopwatch display resolution from the uncertainty introduced by starting and stopping it by hand.
notes: Use the repeated times to estimate the mean and spread. Human reaction time can exceed the instrument’s display increment.
For g = 2s/t², the worst-case fractional uncertainty is Δg/g = Δs/s + 2Δt/t. Quote the calculated acceleration and its uncertainty to consistent decimal places.

notes: Outside a spherical mass, g = GM/r² and F = mg. Add field contributions as vectors when more than one mass is present.
An altitude above a surface is not the radius in the formula: r = R + h. The test mass affects force but not the field strength at its position.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q19:c-time.hint: Draw the velocities with their reference frames labelled. Which two vectors combine to give the required motion?
notes: At non-relativistic speeds, v(A relative to C) = v(A relative to B) + v(B relative to C). Resolve perpendicular directions separately.
For a magnitude and direction, combine the components using Pythagoras and a labelled angle. Do not add the magnitudes of perpendicular velocities.
“From rest” sets the initial velocity to zero. It does not say that the acceleration is zero.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q20:a.hint: If the volume cannot change, which term in the first law disappears?
notes: At constant volume, boundary work pΔV is zero and ΔU = Q. Pressure can still change as the temperature changes.
On a p–V plot the path is vertical, with zero area beneath the volume change. Do not confuse a vertical path with constant pressure.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q20:b.hint: Identify what stays fixed: amount of gas, temperature, pressure or volume. Use only the simplification that those conditions allow.
notes: Use pV = nRT = NkT with absolute pressure and kelvin temperature. For a fixed amount, p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.
If gas leaks or moves between containers, the amount in one container may change. Apply conservation of total molecules to the complete closed system instead of assuming pV/T is fixed locally.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q20:c.hint: Treat the gas as the system and mark the directions of heat and work before substituting numbers.
notes: With W positive for work done by the gas and Q positive into it, ΔU = Q − W. “Rejects heat” makes Q negative; compression makes W negative.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature. An unchanged temperature does not by itself mean no heat or work transfer.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q20:d.hint: Consider the system and its surroundings together. A local entropy decrease need not violate the second law.
notes: For reversible heat transfer at constant temperature, ΔS = Q_rev/T. A warming or cooling reservoir uses the sign of the heat it receives.
The total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease. Irreversible processes increase total entropy and reduce the energy available for useful work; energy itself is still conserved.

notes: For a uniformly rotating coil, flux linkage is NBA cos(ωt) and the emf amplitude is NBAω. The emf is related to the rate of flux change.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q24:whole.hint: Compare atomic and nuclear length scales. A proton belongs to the smaller scale.
notes: Atomic sizes are typically of order 10⁻¹⁰ m, while nucleon dimensions are of order 10⁻¹⁵ m.
For an order-of-magnitude estimate, a factor of two between radius and diameter does not move the answer through several powers of ten.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q25:whole.hint: Connect the particle’s wavelength to its momentum, rather than treating it as a photon.
notes: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. For a non-relativistic particle, p = mv or √(2mE_k).

If accelerated from rest through a voltage magnitude V, E_k = |q|V. Use this only in the non-relativistic regime; E = hc/λ is a photon relation, not a general massive-particle kinetic-energy equation.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q26:nuclear-force.hint: Compare how nuclear mass and nuclear volume depend on nucleon number.
notes: Nuclear radius is approximately R = R₀A^(1/3), while nuclear mass is approximately proportional to A. Volume therefore scales with A.
A is nucleon number and Z is proton number; neutron number is A − Z. Do not confuse the radius of the nucleus with the much larger atomic radius.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q26:electric-force.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q27:energy-flow.hint: Consider the kinetic energy carried by the mass of air reaching the blades each second.
notes: For a uniform wind crossing area A, mass flow rate is ρAv and incoming kinetic power is ½ρAv³.
A working turbine cannot remove all the air’s kinetic energy: air must keep moving away downstream. Include the stated efficiency rather than assuming complete extraction.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q28:a.hint: Identify which objects gain energy and which lose it. Does the temperature change, or is there a change of state?
notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.
For an insulated mixture, energy lost equals energy gained. Include the container’s heat capacity if it is supplied; a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q28:b.hint: Decide whether the question asks for energy over an interval or the rate of transfer at one instant.
notes: Average power is energy transferred / time. Instantaneous mechanical power is P = Fv cos θ.
With a constant driving force, power still changes when speed changes. With constant power, driving force decreases as speed increases.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q28:c.hint: Identify the useful output and the total input before forming a ratio.
notes: Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, or the corresponding power ratio. Both sides must refer to the same interval.
For several stages, multiply the stage efficiencies. Multiply by 100 only when giving a percentage.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q28:d.hint: Follow the energy from its initial store through the turbine and generator.
notes: A tidal barrage uses the gravitational energy of a water-level difference. Flow drives a turbine, and a generator converts mechanical input into electrical output.
For fuel use, mass flow rate = input power / energy per kilogram. Tidal feasibility depends on tidal range, suitable geography, intermittent output and environmental effects.

Escape speed is different from circular orbital speed at the same radius. For ratios, use √(M/R); the escaping object’s mass cancels.

sup-e28d5f281f001dba-w7:c.hint: Draw the direction towards each attracting mass and measure distances from the centres of the masses.
notes: Outside a spherical mass, g = GM/r² and F = mg. Add field contributions as vectors when more than one mass is present.
An altitude above a surface is not the radius in the formula: r = R + h. The test mass affects force but not the field strength at its position.

sup-e28d5f281f001dba-w8:a.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

sup-e28d5f281f001dba-w8:b.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.

sup-e28d5f281f001dba-w10:a.hint: For a uniform stellar disc, compare the area blocked by the planet with the visible stellar area.
notes: In the simple central-transit model, fractional brightness drop = (R_planet/R_star)². Take a square root to obtain the radius ratio.
Mean planetary density is M/(4πR³/3). A non-central transit follows a shorter chord, reducing duration for the same projected speed; limb darkening can modify the simple brightness model.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w1:a.hint: Try placing a positive test charge at a few points to check the proposed field direction.
notes: Electric field lines point from positive towards negative charges, and their tangent gives the local field direction. Closer lines represent a stronger field.
Magnetic field lines form continuous loops. Field lines do not cross, because the field has one direction at each point.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w1:b.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w2:a.hint: Ask whether the required quantity is energy, energy per coulomb, or force per coulomb.
notes: Electric potential is energy per unit charge: V = E_p/q. For a point charge V = kQ/r, and contributions add as signed scalars.
Electric field is perpendicular to equipotentials and points towards decreasing potential. Moving along an equipotential requires no change in electric potential energy.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w2:b.hint: Ask whether the required quantity is energy, energy per coulomb, or force per coulomb.
notes: Electric potential is energy per unit charge: V = E_p/q. For a point charge V = kQ/r, and contributions add as signed scalars.
Electric field is perpendicular to equipotentials and points towards decreasing potential. Moving along an equipotential requires no change in electric potential energy.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w2:c.hint: Ask whether the required quantity is energy, energy per coulomb, or force per coulomb.
notes: Electric potential is energy per unit charge: V = E_p/q. For a point charge V = kQ/r, and contributions add as signed scalars.
Electric field is perpendicular to equipotentials and points towards decreasing potential. Moving along an equipotential requires no change in electric potential energy.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w5:a.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).
A magnetic field alone does no work: the force is perpendicular to velocity. Reverse the force direction for a negative charge.
Link the relevant physical cause to the observation asked about. Naming a law alone does not explain why this particular result follows.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w5:b.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w6:a.hint: For an undeflected particle, compare the two force directions before equating their magnitudes.
notes: With perpendicular electric and magnetic fields arranged to oppose the forces, qE = qvB, so the selected speed is E/B.
Cancellation requires the correct velocity direction as well as speed. A changed speed makes one force dominate; it does not change both forces in the same way.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w6:b.hint: For an undeflected particle, compare the two force directions before equating their magnitudes.
notes: With perpendicular electric and magnetic fields arranged to oppose the forces, qE = qvB, so the selected speed is E/B.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w7:a.hint: Look for a change in magnetic flux linkage, not just the presence of a magnetic field.
notes: Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ for a uniform field, with θ measured from the surface normal. Faraday’s law is ε = −N dΦ/dt.
A changing field, area or orientation can induce an emf. On a flux–time graph use the gradient; a large constant flux by itself gives no emf.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w7:b.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).
A magnetic field alone does no work: the force is perpendicular to velocity. Reverse the force direction for a negative charge.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w7:c.hint: Decide whether the question asks for energy over an interval or the rate of transfer at one instant.
notes: Average power is energy transferred / time. Instantaneous mechanical power is P = Fv cos θ.
With a constant driving force, power still changes when speed changes. With constant power, driving force decreases as speed increases.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w8:a.hint: Look for a change in magnetic flux linkage, not just the presence of a magnetic field.
notes: Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ for a uniform field, with θ measured from the surface normal. Faraday’s law is ε = −N dΦ/dt.
A changing field, area or orientation can induce an emf. On a flux–time graph use the gradient; a large constant flux by itself gives no emf.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w8:b.hint: Decide whether the original flux is increasing or decreasing before choosing the induced field direction.
notes: Lenz’s law makes the induced effect oppose the change in flux. It need not oppose the original field when that field is decreasing.
Use the required induced field direction first, then the right-hand grip rule for conventional current. The opposition is consistent with energy conservation.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w8:c.hint: Ask whether the motion changes flux through a conducting path, and whether induced current can circulate.
notes: Changing flux can drive induced current. Its magnetic effect opposes that flux change, transferring mechanical energy into electrical heating.
Use the direction of entry or exit to determine the induced effect. A uniform field with no changing enclosed flux is not enough by itself to produce a circulating emf.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w9:b.hint: Work out what stays fixed when the circuit changes: voltage, current, or neither.
notes: Electrical power is P = VI. For a resistor this can also be I²R or V²/R; choose the form using known quantities.
Energy transferred is Pt for constant power. A filament lamp’s resistance can change with temperature, so do not assume constant resistance unless stated.

sup-435c2149a36e454d-w10:a.hint: Ask whether the motion changes flux through a conducting path, and whether induced current can circulate.
notes: Changing flux can drive induced current. Its magnetic effect opposes that flux change, transferring mechanical energy into electrical heating.
Use the direction of entry or exit to determine the induced effect. A uniform field with no changing enclosed flux is not enough by itself to produce a circulating emf.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w1:a.hint: Identify what stays fixed: amount of gas, temperature, pressure or volume. Use only the simplification that those conditions allow.
notes: Use pV = nRT = NkT with absolute pressure and kelvin temperature. For a fixed amount, p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.
If gas leaks or moves between containers, the amount in one container may change. Apply conservation of total molecules to the complete closed system instead of assuming pV/T is fixed locally.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w1:b.hint: Translate “isothermal” into a statement about temperature, then consider what that means for an ideal gas’s internal energy.
notes: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, ΔU = 0 and therefore Q = W using work done by the gas. A fixed amount obeys pV = constant.
No temperature change does not mean no heat transfer. Heat can enter during expansion to replace the energy transferred out as work.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w1:c.hint: Translate “isothermal” into a statement about temperature, then consider what that means for an ideal gas’s internal energy.
notes: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, ΔU = 0 and therefore Q = W using work done by the gas. A fixed amount obeys pV = constant.
No temperature change does not mean no heat transfer. Heat can enter during expansion to replace the energy transferred out as work.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w2:a.hint: Link the macroscopic quantity to the random motion and wall collisions of the molecules.
notes: Mean translational kinetic energy is 3kT/2 per molecule. The rms speed obeys v_rms = √(3kT/m), so molecular mass matters when comparing gases.
Pressure comes from the rate of momentum transfer to container walls. In the ideal model, particles have negligible volume and negligible interactions except during elastic collisions.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w2:b.hint: Think about both the rate of wall collisions and the momentum change in each collision.
notes: Gas pressure is momentum transferred to the walls per unit time per unit area. Higher temperature increases typical molecular speeds and momentum transfer.
A smaller volume also increases collision frequency with the walls. Collisions between molecules alone are not the direct force exerted on a wall.
Link the relevant physical cause to the observation asked about. Naming a law alone does not explain why this particular result follows.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w3:a.hint: During a phase change, energy can enter or leave even when the temperature stays the same.
notes: Use Q = mL for the mass that changes phase. Add mcΔT terms only for stages where the material warms or cools within one phase.
A phase change alters intermolecular potential energy; temperature tracks average random kinetic energy. Evaporation can cool the remaining liquid as energetic molecules escape.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w3:b.hint: Think about how energy passes between neighbouring particles, and whether mobile electrons are present.
notes: Conduction transfers energy without bulk movement of matter. In metals, mobile electrons and lattice interactions both contribute; a gas does not have a metallic lattice.
For a steady uniform slab, transfer rate is kAΔT/L. Larger area or temperature difference increases the rate; greater thickness decreases it.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w4:a.hint: Treat the gas as the system and mark the directions of heat and work before substituting numbers.
notes: With W positive for work done by the gas and Q positive into it, ΔU = Q − W. “Rejects heat” makes Q negative; compression makes W negative.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature. An unchanged temperature does not by itself mean no heat or work transfer.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w4:b.hint: Treat the gas as the system and mark the directions of heat and work before substituting numbers.
notes: With W positive for work done by the gas and Q positive into it, ΔU = Q − W. “Rejects heat” makes Q negative; compression makes W negative.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w5:a.hint: Draw the energy entering from the hot reservoir, the useful work and the energy rejected to the cold reservoir.
notes: Over a complete engine cycle ΔU = 0, so W = Q_hot − Q_cold and efficiency = W/Q_hot. Use energy per cycle or power consistently.
Only an ideal reversible Carnot engine reaches η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot. Both reservoir temperatures must be in kelvin; this gives an upper bound for a real engine.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w6:b.hint: Draw the energy entering from the hot reservoir, the useful work and the energy rejected to the cold reservoir.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w7:a.hint: A heat pump uses work to move energy. Identify which heat flow counts as the useful output.
notes: Energy conservation gives Q_hot = Q_cold + W_input. A heating heat pump uses Q_hot/W_input as its coefficient of performance; a refrigerator uses Q_cold/W_input.
A coefficient of performance above one is possible because the device transfers existing thermal energy as well as receiving work. It is not an engine efficiency.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w7:b.hint: A heat pump uses work to move energy. Identify which heat flow counts as the useful output.
notes: Energy conservation gives Q_hot = Q_cold + W_input. A heating heat pump uses Q_hot/W_input as its coefficient of performance; a refrigerator uses Q_cold/W_input.
A coefficient of performance above one is possible because the device transfers existing thermal energy as well as receiving work. It is not an engine efficiency.

A coefficient of performance above one is possible because the device transfers existing thermal energy as well as receiving work. It is not an engine efficiency.

notes: Conduction transfers energy without bulk movement of matter. In metals, mobile electrons and lattice interactions both contribute; a gas does not have a metallic lattice.

notes: Conduction transfers energy without bulk movement of matter. In metals, mobile electrons and lattice interactions both contribute; a gas does not have a metallic lattice.
For a steady uniform slab, transfer rate is kAΔT/L. Larger area or temperature difference increases the rate; greater thickness decreases it.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w9:a.hint: Locate the peak wavelength, rather than the largest wavelength shown on the graph.
notes: Wien’s law is λ_max T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K. Use metres and kelvin; a hotter thermal emitter peaks at a shorter wavelength.
The area under an emission spectrum represents total emitted intensity; the peak position and the peak height are different information.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w9:b.hint: Separate the power emitted by the star from the power received per unit area at the observer.
notes: For isotropic emission, apparent brightness b = L/(4πd²). With parallax p in arcseconds, distance in parsecs is d = 1/p.
In a parallax diagram, p is the half-angle associated with a 1 AU baseline. For brightness ratios, distance enters as a square, so take a square root when solving for distance.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w9:c.hint: Check which way surface temperature increases on the horizontal axis before locating the star.
notes: On a standard H–R diagram luminosity increases upwards and temperature increases to the left. Red giants are luminous but cool; white dwarfs are hot but faint.
Use L = 4πR²σT⁴ to compare radii. A hotter star is not necessarily more luminous, because emitting area also matters.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w10:a.hint: Identify which objects gain energy and which lose it. Does the temperature change, or is there a change of state?
notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.
For an insulated mixture, energy lost equals energy gained. Include the container’s heat capacity if it is supplied; a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C.

sup-79c416eb781dfb14-w10:b.hint: Identify which objects gain energy and which lose it. Does the temperature change, or is there a change of state?
notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w1:a.hint: Check whether the question compares amplitude, intensity, or total power; these do not scale in the same way.
notes: For the same medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. For an isotropic point source, I = P/(4πr²).
When coherent waves overlap, add their signed displacements first and then square the resultant amplitude. Adding intensities alone loses the interference effect.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w1:b.hint: Compare the particle’s displacement direction with the direction in which the wave travels.
notes: Transverse waves have particle oscillations perpendicular to propagation; longitudinal waves have them parallel. Energy travels even though particles oscillate locally.
For a moving wave profile, use a slightly later snapshot to infer the particle’s next displacement. Do not assume a particle moves along the plotted curve.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w1:c.hint: Use the initial displacement and initial direction of motion to decide where the oscillation starts.
notes: For x = A cos(ωt + φ), v = −ωA sin(ωt + φ) and a = −ω²x. Velocity is a quarter-cycle out of phase with displacement.
Read amplitude from the equilibrium line and period between equivalent points. A zero crossing alone does not identify whether the motion is upwards or downwards.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w2:a.hint: Identify whether the diagram shows a snapshot across space or the motion of one point over time.
notes: Use v = fλ and f = 1/T. A spatial separation between equal-phase points gives wavelength; a time separation gives period.
Wave speed is the speed of a disturbance, not the speed of one oscillating particle. Keep the wave’s travel direction separate from the direction of particle motion.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w2:b.hint: Compare the driving frequency with the system’s natural frequency, then consider the damping.
notes: Resonance is a large forced response when the driving frequency is near a natural frequency. Energy must be supplied by the driver.
More damping reduces the peak response and broadens the resonance. Distinguish driving frequency from the free oscillation that would occur without the driver.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w2:c.hint: Mark the boundary conditions at both ends, then fit the simplest allowed pattern between them.
notes: Fixed string ends and closed pipe ends are displacement nodes; an open pipe end is a displacement antinode. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and adjacent antinode are λ/4 apart.
Two like ends allow L = nλ/2. One open and one closed end allows L = (2n − 1)λ/4. Use the mode shown, not automatically the fundamental.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w3:a.hint: Mark the boundary conditions at both ends, then fit the simplest allowed pattern between them.
notes: Fixed string ends and closed pipe ends are displacement nodes; an open pipe end is a displacement antinode. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and adjacent antinode are λ/4 apart.
Two like ends allow L = nλ/2. One open and one closed end allows L = (2n − 1)λ/4. Use the mode shown, not automatically the fundamental.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w3:b.hint: Compare the driving frequency with the system’s natural frequency, then consider the damping.
notes: Resonance is a large forced response when the driving frequency is near a natural frequency. Energy must be supplied by the driver.
More damping reduces the peak response and broadens the resonance. Distinguish driving frequency from the free oscillation that would occur without the driver.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w3:c.hint: Mark the boundary conditions at both ends, then fit the simplest allowed pattern between them.
notes: Fixed string ends and closed pipe ends are displacement nodes; an open pipe end is a displacement antinode. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart; a node and adjacent antinode are λ/4 apart.
Two like ends allow L = nλ/2. One open and one closed end allows L = (2n − 1)λ/4. Use the mode shown, not automatically the fundamental.
Link the relevant physical cause to the observation asked about. Naming a law alone does not explain why this particular result follows.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w4:a.hint: First decide whether the source and observer are getting closer or farther apart.
notes: For sound, source motion changes the spacing of wavefronts; observer motion changes how quickly they are encountered. Choose the Doppler signs so approach increases observed frequency.
For collinear motion, f_obs = f_source(v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source), with speeds measured relative to the medium. Do not simply exchange source and observer speeds.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w4:b.hint: First decide whether the source and observer are getting closer or farther apart.
notes: For sound, source motion changes the spacing of wavefronts; observer motion changes how quickly they are encountered. Choose the Doppler signs so approach increases observed frequency.
For collinear motion, f_obs = f_source(v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source), with speeds measured relative to the medium. Do not simply exchange source and observer speeds.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w4:c.hint: First decide whether the source and observer are getting closer or farther apart.
notes: For sound, source motion changes the spacing of wavefronts; observer motion changes how quickly they are encountered. Choose the Doppler signs so approach increases observed frequency.
For collinear motion, f_obs = f_source(v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source), with speeds measured relative to the medium. Do not simply exchange source and observer speeds.

sup-23e4750e695cc53d-w5:a.hint: Compare the two path lengths to the observation point. Does their difference reinforce or oppose the waves?

ibd-68ce88f733cf3b1d-q12:whole.hint: Connect the energy supplied during the chosen interval to the temperature rise over that same interval.

ibd-68ce88f733cf3b1d-q13:whole.hint: Identify which objects gain energy and which lose it. Does the temperature change, or is there a change of state?
notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.
For an insulated mixture, energy lost equals energy gained. Include the container’s heat capacity if it is supplied; a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C.

ibd-910fb3810eb3dcc6-q2:whole.hint: Try listing the known motion quantities first. Which constant-acceleration equation leaves only the quantity you need?

ibd-910fb3810eb3dcc6-q13:whole.hint: Compare the acceleration with displacement from equilibrium, including its direction.

ibd-910fb3810eb3dcc6-q25:whole.hint: Identify the useful output and the total input before forming a ratio.
notes: Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, or the corresponding power ratio. Both sides must refer to the same interval.

notes: With W positive for work done by the gas and Q positive into it, ΔU = Q − W. “Rejects heat” makes Q negative; compression makes W negative.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature. An unchanged temperature does not by itself mean no heat or work transfer.
